memory_candidates.content: In bash, never accumulate a counter or write to a variable from inside the right-hand side of a `|` pipe -- the pipe's right side runs in a subshell, so any variable mutation there is invisible to the parent shell once the pipe exits (e.g. `producer | while read x; do count=$((count+1)); done` silently leaves `count` unchanged in the caller). Fix by feeding the same loop via process substitution (`done < <(producer)`) instead of a pipe -- this keeps the loop in the current shell so both array/variable mutations persist. For populating an array from a filtered stream while also accumulating a counter, wrap the loop in a function that takes the target array name via `local -n` (nameref) plus operates on a shell-global counter; call it once per array rather than duplicating the loop. Caught by direct manual testing (running the script against a small fixture and checking the counter's actual value) before trusting a test suite's PASS/FAIL alone.

When writing a regression fixture for a probe that has a documented degenerate/zero-candidate branch (e.g. build_errors: null when total_candidates == 0), a fixture that isolates the single behavior under test (e.g. "one file becomes phantom") by using ONLY that one file will often accidentally trigger the degenerate branch instead of the intended non-degenerate assertion, because removing the only candidate makes total_candidates hit zero. Always add an untouched, valid companion candidate to such a fixture so the candidate total stays nonzero and the fixture actually exercises the intended branch -- verify by checking the fixture's actual output against expectations, not just that the code compiles or the fixture 'looks right' on paper. This applies to both regression-suite fixtures and ad hoc before/after acceptance-evidence fixtures.
